newsitem.title: USA: US not too vulnerable to slow Japan growth--Shafer.
newsitem.headline: US not too vulnerable to slow Japan growth--Shafer.

text.p: The rapid rise of emerging market economies has made the United States less vulnerable to slowdowns in Japan and Europe, but there are some risks, outgoing Treasury Undersecretary Jeffrey Shafer said Thursday.
"We're not that vulnerable partly because the centers of growth of the world have spread out," he told Reuters.

Shafer, who is joining Wall Street broker Salomon Brothers on Feb. 1, said one of the more satisfying parts of his job at Treasury had been shifting the department's international focus more to the emerging markets of Asia and Latin America.

Shafer said the biggest threat to the global economy during his time at Treasury came not from developments in industrial nations, but from the 1994/95 Mexican currency crisis that threatened to spill over into other emerging market economies.

Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin praised Shafer for his "critical leadership role" in arranging the rescue package for Mexico. Mexico this week repaid the remaining money borrowed from the United States under that package.
"Mexico stands out as the emotionally absorbing thing that came out well and was right (during my time in Treasury)," Shafer said.

Shafer ackowledged that the rapid rise of emerging markets may have allowed the United States to be a bit more relaxed about the "disappointing" economic performance of Europe and Japan of recent years. But that posture also reflects a recognition of the limits of what can be achieved through macroeconomic policy and an increased focus on the medium term among the Group of Seven industrial nations, he said.

"We no longer see macroeconomic policy as a matter of fine-tuning from one month to the next," Shafer said. "(But) there have been, and will presumably be occasions again when we will want to intervene in markets," he added.
Shafer said the United States has emphasized continuity in its dollar policy because it has been comfortable with developments in the currency markets.

"There's been a period for some time when people are reasonably comfortable and the right thing to do has been to emphasize continuity," he said. "That's something we have done," he added, echoing Rubin's strong dollar policy.
He said there is a recognition that the authorities cannot control the currency markets. But that does not mean pursuing a totally hands-off approach.

Shafer, who has been heavily involved in multilateral talks on financial service deregulation while at Treasury, said he believes that the Japanese government was committed to carrying out its planned "Big Bang" of financial reforms.
While the "inertial forces" in Japan are very strong, there is a will for the government to move ahead, he said.
Shafer acknowledged that the recent steep drop in the Tokyo stock market posed problems for Japanese banks, which count heavily on their equity investments for capital.
"If the market goes down and stays down, they have more of a problem rebuilding capotal," he said. "But I don't think that brings on instability."
